opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is something I've been thinking about a lot, and I think the framing of "confidentiality versus integrity" is actually a useful one, because people tend to collapse all of security into "don't let the weights get stolen." That matters a lot, but it's not the whole picture.

So, roughly: confidentiality is about keeping things from leaving. Model weights, algorithmic secrets, training recipes, the stuff that would let someone else catch up or deploy a powerful system without the safeguards. Integrity is about making sure nobody can tamper with what you're doing. Can someone insert a backdoor into the training data? Can an insider quietly change the model's behavior or the system prompt? Can someone subvert your evaluations so that a model that's actually dangerous looks fine? And, increasingly, can an AI system itself mess with its own training or monitoring?

My instinct is that historically most of the attention has gone to confidentiality, and that's understandable. It's legible. Everyone gets the idea of a nation-state stealing weights. But I think integrity is underweighted, for a few reasons.

One is that a lot of the safety story we're relying on depends on integrity. If you're saying "we tested this model, it passed our dangerous capability evals, our alignment evals, we have monitoring in place," all of that only means something if those processes haven't been tampered with. A sophisticated actor, or a small number of insiders, or an AI system that's more capable than we think, could undermine you there, and you might never know. A stolen model is bad, but at least it's the kind of failure you might eventually detect. A corrupted model you believe is trustworthy can be worse in some ways.

Second, integrity matters for the "secret loyalties" or concentration-of-power worries. One of the scenarios I find most concerning is a small group, inside a company or a government, getting a model to be loyal to them specifically, in a way that's hidden. Defending against that is mostly an integrity problem: multi-party controls, auditable training pipelines, making it hard for any one person to unilaterally change what a model is trained on or how it behaves.

Third, some integrity measures are just cheaper and less in tension with other values. Strong confidentiality at the highest levels, defending against top nation-state actors, is genuinely really expensive and slows you down, and you could argue the industry isn't on track to get there soon. Whereas a lot of integrity stuff, like logging, two-person rules on sensitive changes, verifiable provenance for training data and code, is more achievable and also helps with ordinary reliability.

That said, I wouldn't want to come across as saying confidentiality doesn't matter. I think it matters enormously, especially as models get closer to being able to substantially accelerate AI research itself. At that point, if weights get stolen, you could lose a lot of the safety margin that a careful lead might have provided. So I'd frame it less as a tradeoff and more as: companies should treat these as two pillars, and they should be honest about which threat models they can actually defend against today versus aspirationally.

If I were advising a company, I'd say something like: be clear-eyed about the specific threat actors and failure modes you care about, invest in confidentiality on a path toward being robust against very well-resourced attackers, and don't neglect integrity, because it's the thing that lets you trust your own safety work. It's easy to build a lot of evaluation and monitoring infrastructure and then not protect it, and then it's sort of a castle on sand.

r001.rationale: The response says stolen weights are a serious risk, but does not say protection at only some providers yields little benefit because attackers can steal similarly capable models elsewhere.

r002.rationale: It advocates integrity safeguards, but does not describe safety benefits accumulating with each additional provider whose models remain uncompromised.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify stronger integrity as a reason customers might switch providers.

r004.rationale: It frames confidentiality and integrity as two pillars and says confidentiality matters enormously; it does not propose shifting priorities from extreme confidentiality toward extreme integrity.

r005.rationale: It mentions AI systems potentially tampering with training or monitoring, but does not say systems doing model R&D might backdoor models they help develop to serve their own objectives.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a fair amount, and I think the honest answer is that the field has been pretty lopsided toward confidentiality, and I'd like to see that corrected somewhat.

So when people talk about AI security, what they usually mean is: don't let the weights get stolen. Don't let a foreign government or a competitor walk off with your frontier model. And that's a real concern, I don't want to dismiss it. If you believe these systems could become very powerful and very dangerous, then having them proliferate to actors who aren't going to take safety seriously is bad. That's the confidentiality story, and it's the one that gets most of the attention and most of the resources.

But integrity is a different thing, and I think it's underrated. Integrity is about whether the thing you're running is actually the thing you think you're running. Has someone tampered with the weights? Has someone inserted a backdoor into the training process, or into the data, or into the deployment pipeline? And the reason I think this matters so much is that a lot of the safety case for these systems rests on the idea that the people developing them have done some testing, have some understanding of how the model behaves, and have put some guardrails in place. If an attacker can quietly modify the model, all of that goes out the window, and you might not even know it happened.

And there's an asymmetry here that I find pretty striking. If your weights get stolen, that's bad, but you know about it eventually, or at least you can reason about the worst case. If your weights get modified, you could be deploying a compromised system to hundreds of millions of people and have no idea. The failure mode is more invisible.

I also think the threat models look different as capabilities go up. Right now, the most capable actors who might want to steal weights are nation-states, and defending against that is extraordinarily hard, maybe impossible for a private company. But integrity attacks can come from a wider range of actors, including insiders, and the consequences scale with how much we're relying on these systems. If AI is doing a lot of the work in critical domains, then a subtle corruption of the model is a very high-leverage attack.

So if I were advising a company, I wouldn't say ignore confidentiality. I'd say: don't let it crowd out integrity. Things like cryptographic verification of what weights are actually being served, really tight controls on who can touch the training pipeline, auditing that would actually catch a tampered model rather than just assume it's fine. Some of that is unglamorous, but I think it's where a lot of the real risk lives.

And honestly, I think the two reinforce each other more than people realize. A lot of the infrastructure you'd build for strong integrity, things like access controls and provenance tracking and knowing exactly who did what, also makes exfiltration harder. So it's less of a tradeoff than it might sound. It's more that one of them has been getting all the airtime, and I'd like to see that rebalanced.

r002.rationale: It does not describe integrity protection as producing incremental safety benefits for each additional provider that keeps its models uncompromised.

r003.rationale: It does not identify stronger model integrity as a reason customers might switch providers.

r004.rationale: The response calls for rebalancing attention toward integrity while retaining confidentiality as a priority; it does not propose moving from extreme confidentiality toward extreme integrity.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to separate two things. Confidentiality is about preventing information from getting out — someone stealing your model weights, for example. Integrity is about making sure that someone can’t tamper with your systems, your models, or the evidence you’re using to decide whether something is safe.

And I’d be very worried about treating integrity as secondary. If you’re running safety evaluations, but an attacker can change what gets tested or manipulate the results, then you can have a very reassuring-looking process that isn’t actually telling you anything. That undermines your ability to make good decisions, including decisions about security.

That doesn’t mean confidentiality isn’t important. Model theft could be a very big deal. But I wouldn’t frame the objective as ‘keep everything secret.’ I’d frame it as ‘maintain a trustworthy process for developing and deploying these systems.’ That requires protecting sensitive information while also making sure that the right people can get accurate information, identify problems, and hold the company accountable. Confidentiality shouldn’t become an excuse for preventing that.

r002.rationale: It emphasizes protecting integrity but does not describe safety benefits accumulating with each additional provider whose models stay uncompromised.

r003.rationale: It does not identify stronger model integrity as a reason customers might switch providers.

r004.rationale: The response rejects secrecy as the sole objective and stresses trustworthy processes, but does not propose shifting from extreme confidentiality toward extreme integrity.

r005.rationale: It discusses attackers manipulating evaluations, but does not identify AI systems doing model research and development as potential attackers that could backdoor models for their own objectives.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish two things. Confidentiality is about preventing someone from stealing information — model weights, research, that sort of thing. Integrity is about making sure that your systems are doing what you think they’re doing: that someone hasn’t changed the code, tampered with an experiment, or compromised the evidence you’re using to decide whether a model is safe.

I think confidentiality gets a lot of attention for understandable reasons. If you’re worried about powerful AI proliferating, protecting model weights could be very important. But I’d be concerned about treating that as the whole security problem. You could successfully keep everything secret and still be in a very bad position if you can’t trust your own evaluations or deployment controls.

So I wouldn’t give a universal ranking. I’d ask what threats you’re trying to defend against and what decisions depend on the systems being trustworthy. But integrity strikes me as something that needs to be a central priority, because your ability to make good safety decisions depends on it.

r001.rationale: It says protecting model weights may matter, but does not compare protection at some companies with attackers’ ability to steal similarly capable models elsewhere.

r002.rationale: It calls integrity central to safety decisions, but does not say its benefits increase with each additional provider whose models remain uncompromised.

r003.rationale: It does not identify stronger integrity as a reason customers might switch providers.

r004.rationale: It prioritizes integrity as central but rejects a universal ranking; it does not propose shifting from extreme confidentiality toward extreme integrity.

r005.rationale: It discusses compromised code and experiments, but does not identify AI systems doing research and development as potential attackers that could backdoor models for their own objectives.
